sections.title: Tras, después and luego
sections.text: Tras directly introduces a complement: tras la reunión or tras comer. Después uses de before a noun or infinitive and can stand alone. Luego can also stand alone; luego de is used with regional variation. All can describe temporal succession, but their sentence structures differ.

sections.title: Then: next, or at that time?
sections.text: Entonces can refer back to a time already mentioned. Después and luego can instead place an event later. Entonces also introduces an inference, much like then or in that case.
examples: En 2020 vivía en Lima. Entonces trabajaba allí.
In 2020 I lived in Lima. At that time I worked there.
¿No hay trenes? Entonces iremos en autobús.
There are no trains? Then we’ll go by bus.

sections.title: Behind and in pursuit
sections.text: Tras also has spatial and pursuit senses. It is not simply a formal replacement for every use of después. The complement and intended relationship determine the meaning.
examples: El jardín está tras la casa.
The garden is behind the house.
El perro corre tras la pelota.
The dog runs after the ball.

sections.title: The shared meaning
sections.text: Empezar and comenzar both express the beginning of an action or event. Either can take a direct object or describe an event beginning. Ordinary beginning sentences often do not select just one of them.
examples: La clase empieza a las nueve.
La clase comienza a las nueve.

sections.title: Starting an action
sections.text: Both take a + infinitive to say that an action begins. Keep the a: it connects the beginning verb to the action.

sections.title: What you do first
sections.text: Empezar por + infinitive and comenzar por + infinitive name the first step in a sequence. This differs from a + infinitive, which simply presents the onset of the action.
examples: We start by reading the instructions.
We start by reading the instructions.
sources: University of Santiago de Compostela · verb constructions

sections.title: Register and regional preference
sections.text: A 2025 corpus study reports a tendency toward comenzar in formal and written use and empezar in informal and spoken use, with differences between countries. This is a preference, not a rule making the other verb incorrect in an ordinary sentence.

sections.title: Useful forms
sections.text: Both change e to ie in forms such as yo empiezo / comienzo. In the first-person singular simple past, z changes to c before é: empecé / comencé. Learn the corresponding forms together.
examples: I start today; I started yesterday.
I begin today; I began yesterday.

sections.title: Facts, familiarity and understanding
sections.text: Saber is the usual choice for knowing a fact or how to do something. Conocer is useful for acquaintance with people and familiarity with places. Entender and comprender express comprehension. These are starting points: the words also overlap in some knowledge senses.

sections.title: Knowing how
sections.text: Saber + infinitive means having a learned ability. Poder + infinitive can instead express ability, possibility or permission in the circumstances. A person can know how to swim and still be unable to swim right now.
examples: Sé nadar, pero hoy no puedo nadar.
I know how to swim, but I can’t swim today.

sections.title: Where saber and conocer overlap
sections.text: Both can concern information someone possesses. A useful contrast is Sé la respuesta and Conozco la respuesta: both can mean I know the answer. Knowing a fact about a person is different from knowing that person personally.
examples: Sé quién es Ana, pero no la conozco.
I know who Ana is, but I don’t know her personally.

sections.title: Meeting someone
sections.text: Conocer can describe becoming acquainted with someone. In a completed past event, it can therefore translate as meet. Encontrarse con alguien can describe an encounter with someone already known; meeting in English does not automatically select conocer.
examples: Conocí a Ana en un curso.
I met Ana on a course.
Me encontré con Ana en la estación.
I ran into Ana at the station.

sections.title: Entender and comprender
sections.text: Both work for grasping an explanation, and both can express understanding another person. There is no reliable rule that entender is always superficial while comprender is always deep or emotional.

sections.title: Constructions and additional senses
sections.text: Entender de + subject expresses knowledge or expertise. Comprender can also mean include or comprise. Saber a + something describes taste. These senses belong to the individual verbs; they do not transfer to every near-synonym.

sections.title: Belief, reflection and feeling
sections.text: Creer can present something as true or likely. Pensar can describe reflection and also an opinion. Sentir covers physical sensations and emotions, and can also express an impression. An opinion sentence may allow more than one of these verbs.

sections.title: Considering and seeming
sections.text: Considerar can mean examine something or judge it to have a quality. Parecer expresses an appearance or impression; me parece marks the impression as mine. Pensar + infinitive can express an intention.
examples: It seems like a good idea to me.

sections.title: Identity and a presented state
sections.text: Ser identifies or classifies and attributes characteristics. Estar presents a state or condition, often associated with a situation or result. Permanent versus temporary is not a reliable universal test.

sections.title: The adjective can change meaning
sections.text: The choice can change what an adjective conveys. Ser listo describes intelligence; estar listo describes readiness. Ser nuevo says something is new; estar nuevo can say it is in like-new condition.

sections.title: Location
sections.text: Estar locates people and things, including places with stable locations. For the place where an event takes place, Spanish uses ser.
examples: La reunión es en mi casa.
The meeting is at my house.

sections.title: Three points of reference
sections.text: A basic spatial contrast is este near the speaker, ese near the listener or at some distance from the speaker, and aquel distant from both. Speakers also use them to organize time and references in conversation.
examples: That building over there in the distance.

sections.title: Agreement and neutral forms
sections.text: Este, ese and aquel vary with the noun: esta casa, esos libros, aquellas personas. Esto, eso and aquello are neutral forms for something unspecified, a situation or an idea; they do not go directly before a noun.

sections.title: Cause, purpose and recipient
sections.text: Por can give the cause or motive; para can give the intended purpose or recipient. Both may translate as for. The relationship matters more than the English preposition.
examples: They closed because of the rain.
I study in order to learn.

sections.title: Route, exchange and deadlines
sections.text: Por can introduce a route, price or exchange, and a communication channel. Para can point to a destination or deadline. These are additional uses, so the cause/purpose distinction does not explain every sentence.
examples: Pagué diez euros por el libro.
I paid ten euros for the book.

sections.title: Leaving a place or leaving something
sections.text: Salir de focuses on going out of a place. Irse focuses on departing. Dejar can take the person, place or thing being left as its object; it does not require physically going outside in every use.
examples: I go out of the office.

sections.title: Stopping and allowing
sections.text: Dejar de + infinitive means stop doing something. Dejar + infinitive can mean allow an action. The presence of de changes the construction.

sections.title: Getting a result
sections.text: Lograr presents achieving what was sought. Conseguir can likewise mean obtain or succeed in doing something. Obtener means obtain a result or thing. An achievement need not be heroic or especially difficult.
examples: She managed to finish on time.
She managed to finish on time.

sections.title: Construction and point of view
sections.text: Lograr and conseguir directly take an infinitive for succeeding in an action. Obtener does not take that same direct-infinitive construction. Recibir presents something arriving or being given to someone; tener presents possession or a state.
examples: I have a letter for you.

sections.title: Still, already and no longer
sections.text: Aún and todavía overlap when something continues. Ya often marks a change as reached; ya no marks a state as no longer true. Aún no and todavía no mean not yet.

sections.title: The accent matters
sections.text: Aún has an accent when it has the value of todavía, including intensification such as aún más. Aun without it can mean even, including or even though in constructions such as aun cuando.

sections.title: Having and there being
sections.text: Tener expresses possession and states such as age or hunger. Existential haber says there is or there are. In standard Spanish this impersonal haber remains singular even with a plural noun.

sections.title: An auxiliary versus exist
sections.text: Haber also builds compound tenses with a participle. Existir is an ordinary verb meaning exist and agrees with its subject.

groups.title: ir · pasar · llegar · volver · salir · venir · entrar

sections.title: Direction and stages of a journey
sections.text: Ir presents going, venir movement toward the speaker or another adopted reference point. Llegar focuses on arrival, entrar on entry and salir on exit. A destination after ir does not mean arrival has already occurred.
examples: I arrived at the hotel and went in.

sections.title: Passing and returning
sections.text: Pasar can mean pass or go through/by a place. Volver can mean return. Volver a + infinitive instead means do something again.

sections.title: What remains, and what continues
sections.text: Quedar can describe something left over; quedarse can describe staying. Seguir can mean follow or continue. Seguir + gerund presents an action as ongoing.

sections.title: State and maintenance
sections.text: Estar describes a state. Mantener can mean keep something in a state; mantenerse presents the subject remaining in it. These can describe related situations with different grammatical roles.

groups.title: dar · dejar · llevar · poner · tomar · recibir

sections.title: Moving, placing and leaving
sections.text: Llevar can mean carry or take something to a place. Traer means bring toward the place of speaking or a place adopted as reference. Poner places something; dejar can leave it there.
examples: Llevo los libros a la escuela.
I take the books to school.
Pon el libro en la mesa.
Put the book on the table.

sections.title: Taking, giving and receiving
sections.text: Tomar can mean take or grasp, and also drink or take transport. Dar and recibir describe opposite roles in a transfer. English take covers too many relationships to select one Spanish verb without context.
examples: Le doy un regalo y ella lo recibe.
I give her a gift and she receives it.

sections.title: Doing, creating and carrying out
sections.text: Hacer is broad: do or make. Realizar can mean carry out an action or plan. Crear highlights bringing something into existence; producir can highlight an output or effect. These uses overlap rather than forming separate categories for every object.

sections.title: Producing and transforming
sections.text: Producir can describe manufacture or causing an effect. Convertir algo en otra cosa means turn something into something else. Convertirse en presents the subject undergoing that change.
examples: Convirtieron la casa en un museo.
They turned the house into a museum.

sections.title: Seeing and directing your gaze
sections.text: Ver presents visual perception. Mirar presents directing the gaze or attention. Both can describe watching in appropriate contexts; television is not a universal dividing line.
examples: Miro por la ventana, pero no veo nada.
I look through the window, but I don’t see anything.

sections.title: Feeling and other meanings
sections.text: Sentir can express sensations, emotions and regret. Ver can also mean understand or recognize something; perception verbs are not restricted to a single physical sense.

sections.title: Showing and introducing
sections.text: Mostrar and enseñar can both mean show something so it can be seen. Presentar can introduce a person or put something before someone for consideration.
examples: Let me introduce you to Ana.

sections.title: Teaching and submitting
sections.text: Enseñar also means teach. Presentar can describe presenting or submitting a document or proposal. These meanings do not automatically carry over from the shared show sense.

sections.title: Content, conversation and narration
sections.text: Decir presents what is said; hablar presents speaking or conversation. Contar can mean tell or recount a story, and also count. Hablar de names the topic of conversation.

sections.title: Calling and explaining
sections.text: Llamar can mean call by phone, summon or give a name. Llamarse gives someone’s name. Explicar presents making something understandable, rather than merely saying it.

sections.title: Asking for information or requesting something
sections.text: Preguntar asks a question or seeks information. Pedir asks to receive something or have something done. A request for an explanation uses pedir even though the thing requested is information.
examples: I asked what time it was.

sections.title: The clause after the verb
sections.text: Preguntar si can introduce whether something is true. Pedir que + subjunctive asks someone to do something. Preguntar por alguien asks about that person; pedir hablar con alguien requests a conversation.
examples: She asked whether Ana was there.

sections.title: Searching does not guarantee finding
sections.text: Buscar is the search or attempt; encontrar is finding or encountering. Encontrar does not require a prior search.
examples: Busqué las llaves, pero no las encontré.
I looked for the keys, but I didn’t find them.
Encontré una moneda en la calle.
I found a coin in the street.

sections.title: Acquaintance and encounters
sections.text: Conocer can mean know personally or become acquainted. Encontrarse con can describe meeting or running into someone. Encontrarse also describes a state or location.
examples: I met Luis for the first time yesterday.

sections.title: Wanting, hoping, expecting and waiting
sections.text: Querer means want and can express affection. Esperar can mean wait, hope or expect. The complement and situation identify which meaning is intended.

sections.title: When another person acts
sections.text: Querer que and esperar que commonly introduce subjunctive clauses for a desired or hoped-for action by someone else. Querer + infinitive gives the action the subject wants to do.

sections.title: Ability, possibility and permission
sections.text: Poder + infinitive can express ability or possibility and can ask permission. Dejar and permitir can give permission or allow an event. Permitir can also describe something making an action possible.
examples: La llave permite abrir la puerta.
The key allows the door to be opened.

sections.title: Obligation, probability and owing
sections.text: Deber + infinitive is the usual form for obligation. Deber de + infinitive usually expresses probability; deber without de also commonly has that meaning. The current DPD also accepts occasional obligation uses with de. Do not treat de as an infallible test. Deber + a noun can mean owe.

sections.title: The complement changes tratar
sections.text: Tratar de + infinitive can mean try to do something. With a topic, tratar de can mean be about. Tratar a alguien describes treatment of a person; tratar una enfermedad means treat an illness.

sections.title: Discussing or considering
sections.text: Hablar de describes speaking about a topic. Considerar can describe examining an option or judging something a certain way. These actions may occur together, but the verbs highlight different things.

sections.title: Origin and starting point
sections.text: De links origin, possession, material and many other relationships. Desde emphasizes a starting point in space or time.
examples: La mesa de Ana es de madera.
Ana’s table is made of wood.
I have worked here since January.

sections.title: Naming both ends
sections.text: De…a and desde…hasta can mark the endpoints of a span; desde…a also exists. Do not learn a rule that a can only pair with de. The whole phrase expresses the range.
examples: Desde la puerta hasta la ventana.
From the door to the window.

sections.title: Destination and direction
sections.text: A commonly names a destination; hacia emphasizes direction toward it. Para can also introduce a destination. None of these alone proves that arrival has occurred.

sections.title: Other uses of a
sections.text: A also marks a time, some indirect objects and certain human direct objects. These uses do not mean physical movement toward a place. A + el contracts to al.
examples: La clase es a las nueve.

sections.title: Position in context
sections.text: En can mean in, on or at. Sobre can mean on or above. Dentro means inside and usually takes de before a named place. Entre expresses between or among.
examples: El libro está en la mesa.
The book is on the table.
La lámpara está sobre la mesa.
The lamp is above the table.

sections.title: Position versus subject matter
sections.text: Sobre also introduces a subject or topic. De can introduce a topic too. Dentro can stand alone when the place is understood.

sections.title: Earlier in time
sections.text: Antes can stand alone or take de before a noun or infinitive. Before a clause, both antes de que and antes que exist.

sections.title: In front of, in the presence of, faced with
sections.text: Ante directly introduces someone or something: a judge, an audience, or a circumstance faced. It is not the ordinary substitute for temporal antes de.

sections.title: A period or a simultaneous action
sections.text: Durante takes a noun naming a period or event. Mientras can introduce a clause describing something happening at the same time. Cuando places an event at a time or occasion.
examples: I call you when I arrive.

sections.title: Mientras que
sections.text: Mientras que can compare contrasting situations, and also has temporal uses. For an unambiguously simultaneous reading, plain mientras is a useful basic construction. Mientras can also mean meanwhile when the other event is understood.
examples: Ana cocina, mientras que Luis prefiere pedir comida.
Ana cooks, whereas Luis prefers to order food.

sections.title: Connecting and adding
sections.text: Y connects elements. También adds a parallel fact or participant. Además introduces additional information; these roles overlap in some sentences but their syntax differs.
examples: Ana is coming. Luis is too.
It is useful and, moreover, cheap.

sections.title: Besides something
sections.text: Además de introduces the thing or action to which something is added. También does not take de in this construction.

sections.title: Giving the reason
sections.text: Porque can give the reason. Causal como presents a background reason before the consequence. Causal pues normally follows what it explains. Initial Pues… can instead be a discourse response, so position alone does not classify every pues.
examples: We’re not going out because it’s raining.
Since it’s raining, we’re not going out.
We’re not going out, since it’s raining.

sections.title: Drawing a conclusion
sections.text: Entonces can mean then or in that case. Luego can mean therefore. Pues also has a consequence use and a conversational well use. These differ from naming an earlier cause.
examples: No hay trenes; entonces iremos en autobús.
There are no trains; then we’ll go by bus.
Todos están de acuerdo; podemos, pues, empezar.
Everyone agrees; we can therefore begin.

sections.title: Contrast or replacement
sections.text: Pero presents a contrast. Sino usually replaces something explicitly denied. Before a full clause with a conjugated verb, use sino que.
examples: I don’t want tea, but coffee.
She didn’t call; she wrote instead.

sections.title: Concession and if not
sections.text: Aunque can mean although or even if. Indicative can assert the circumstance as a fact; subjunctive can present it as hypothetical or not what is being asserted. Si no is the two-word sequence if not, distinct from sino.
examples: Although it is raining, we’re going out.
Even if it rains, we’ll go out.

groups.title: que · como · cuando · qué · donde · quien · cómo · cual

sections.title: Connecting a description
sections.text: Relative que can refer to people or things. Quien refers to people and is especially useful after a preposition or in supplementary clauses. El cual, la cual and their plurals are also relative forms; the surrounding construction determines where they fit.
examples: The person with whom I spoke.
Ana, quien vive aquí, me ayudó.
Ana, who lives here, helped me.

sections.title: A question inside a sentence
sections.text: Qué and cómo have accents in both direct and indirect questions. Que can also introduce a statement. Donde, cuando and como have corresponding question forms dónde, cuándo and cómo.
examples: I don’t know what she wants.
I know that she wants to come.

groups.title: se · lo · le · me · él · nos · te · yo · mí

sections.title: The role determines the form
sections.text: Yo is a subject form, me an unstressed object form, and mí follows many prepositions. The same role distinction helps with él, lo/le, te and nos. Lo commonly marks a masculine singular direct object, le an indirect object.
examples: I give him or her the book.

sections.title: Se and regional qualifications
sections.text: Se can be reflexive or reciprocal, form impersonal or passive constructions, or replace le/les before lo/la/los/las. Standard Spanish also accepts le for a singular male person as direct object in the leísmo described by the DPD; it is not freely interchangeable with lo everywhere.
examples: I give it to him or her.

sections.title: Owner and owned item
sections.text: Mío relates to me, tuyo to tú/vos, nuestro to us. Suyo can refer to him, her, them, usted or ustedes. The ending agrees with what is owned, not with the owner’s gender.
examples: The house is his, hers, theirs or yours.

sections.title: Before the noun and clarification
sections.text: Use mi libro, tu libro and su libro before the noun; nuestro retains its agreeing form, as in nuestra casa. To clarify the owner of suyo, use a phrase such as de ella or de ustedes.
examples: Es su libro: el libro de ella.
It is her book: the book belonging to her.

groups.title: el · que · como · él · si · qué · cómo · sí

sections.title: Small accent, different function
sections.text: El is an article; él is a pronoun. Si introduces if or whether; sí can mean yes or be a reflexive form after a preposition. Mi is possessive; mí follows many prepositions.
examples: If she comes, tell her yes.
Mi libro es importante para mí.
My book is important to me.

sections.title: Questions need no question marks to keep their accents
sections.text: Question words retain their accents inside indirect questions. Compare an assertion introduced by que with a question introduced by qué; compare como for as/like with cómo for how.
examples: I know that she is coming.
I don’t know what she wants.
I don’t know how to do it.

sections.title: A, one and someone
sections.text: Un is used before a masculine singular noun; uno can stand alone as a number or pronoun. The article and numeral can have the same surface form, with context establishing whether one is being emphasized.
examples: I have a book / one book.

sections.title: Only, alone and unique
sections.text: Solo as an adverb means only. As an adjective, solo/sola can mean alone. Único/única means sole or unique and agrees with its noun.

groups.title: todo · otro · alguno · mucho · cada · algo · nada · poco · varios · ninguno · cualquiera

sections.title: Whole, each and unspecified members
sections.text: Todo can cover a whole or all members. Cada distributes over members or intervals. Alguno introduces an unspecified member; cualquiera allows an unrestricted choice. Algún, ningún and cualquier are forms used before certain nouns.

sections.title: Amount and negative expressions
sections.text: Mucho and poco can describe amounts; their forms agree with a noun. Algunos and varios overlap without a precise numerical boundary. Algo and nada refer to something and nothing. Negatives after a verb commonly accompany no; before it, they can supply the negation themselves.
examples: Hay mucha agua y pocos vasos.
There is a lot of water and there are few glasses.

groups.title: más · muy · mucho · tan · menos · casi · tanto

sections.title: Very, a lot and so much
sections.text: Muy precedes an ordinary adjective or adverb. Mucho modifies an action, quantifies a noun with agreement, and intensifies comparatives such as mejor or más. Tan and tanto show a related difference.

sections.title: More, less, almost and equal degree
sections.text: Más and menos compare quantity or degree. Casi means almost and does not express a high degree by itself. Tan…como compares qualities; tanto…como can compare an amount or an action.
examples: Necesito más tiempo y menos ruido.
I need more time and less noise.
He is as tall as Ana.
I work as much as you.

sections.title: Good and well
sections.text: Bueno describes a noun, with agreement; buen is used before a masculine singular noun. Bien often describes how an action is done. With estar, bien can describe being well or something being okay.

sections.title: Better and intensification
sections.text: Mejor can compare good or well. Bien can also intensify an adjective. A broad English gloss good is therefore not enough to determine the grammatical form.

sections.title: Different dimensions
sections.text: Grande describes size broadly, alto height, largo length or duration. Pequeño describes small size and can also refer to young age. Grande before a singular noun often becomes gran and can convey greatness.

sections.title: Age and comparison
sections.text: Mayor can mean larger or greater, or older in an age comparison. It also has noncomparative age senses such as grown-up or elderly. It is not a universal replacement for más grande in every physical-size sentence.
examples: Mi hermana es mayor que yo.
My sister is older than me.

sections.title: Same, another and own
sections.text: Mismo identifies the same thing or expresses sameness. Otro introduces something different or additional. Propio can express one’s own possession or something characteristic of a person or thing.

sections.title: Emphasis and uniqueness
sections.text: Mismo after a personal pronoun adds emphasis: the person themself. Único says something is the sole one or unique; it does not simply mean the same.

sections.title: Time as duration or occurrence
sections.text: Tiempo names time or duration; vez counts an occurrence. Hora can mean a sixty-minute unit or a clock time. Día names a day.

sections.title: A moment, an occasion and weather
sections.text: Momento can mean a brief interval or a particular occasion, including a broader period defined by events. Tiempo also means weather. Learn these as senses of the word rather than substitutes for every English time.

sections.title: Activity, employment and a result
sections.text: Trabajo is a noun for work, a job or a piece of work. Trabajar is the verb. Obra can name a created work, including art or construction, and sometimes overlaps with trabajo.

sections.title: Studying, a study and a studio
sections.text: Estudio can mean study as an activity, a particular investigation or a studio. Its translation depends on the construction. Obra can also name a play or building work.

groups.title: persona · mujer · hombre · niño · hijo · gente · humano

sections.title: People, age and family relationship
sections.text: Persona is an individual. Niño/niña describes a child’s age; hijo/hija describes a relationship to a parent and can refer to an adult. Mujer can mean woman or wife; hombre can mean man and also human being in some uses.
examples: My daughter is thirty years old.

sections.title: Gente and agreement
sections.text: In general Spanish, gente is a feminine singular collective noun. Some American varieties also use it as a count noun for individuals. Persona is grammatically feminine regardless of the person referred to; humano can be an adjective or a noun.

sections.title: Shape or way of doing something
sections.text: Forma can mean physical shape or manner. Manera and modo also describe how something is done. Their manner senses often overlap.
examples: It is another way of learning.
It is another way of learning.

sections.title: Kind and classification
sections.text: Tipo and clase can classify things into kinds. They need not describe the procedure used to do something. Tipo also has other senses, including a person in colloquial speech.
examples: What kind of music do you like?
What kind of problem is it?

sections.title: State and situation
sections.text: Estado and situación overlap for a condition or set of circumstances. There is no dependable rule dividing internal estado from external situación. The words also have specialized senses.
examples: El coche está en buen estado.
The car is in good condition.

sections.title: A case, and other senses of state
sections.text: Caso can describe a particular instance, matter or investigation. Estado can name a political state; situación can name location. A shared English word does not transfer all these senses.
examples: En este caso, es mejor esperar.
In this case, it is better to wait.

groups.title: parte · lugar · punto · centro · nivel · lado

sections.title: Location, portion and side
sections.text: Lugar is a place; parte can be a portion or part; lado a side. All have extended uses, so general location phrases can overlap.

sections.title: Point, center and level
sections.text: Punto can mean a dot, a point on a route, a score point or a matter under discussion. Centro names a center or an institution. Nivel can describe height, a level or a degree.
examples: Este es el punto de encuentro.

sections.title: A group and a team
sections.text: Grupo is a collection of people or things. Equipo can mean a team organized for an activity. A team is also a group; the distinction concerns what the word highlights.

sections.title: Equipment and conjunto
sections.text: Equipo also means equipment. Conjunto can mean a set or collection and can name a sports team. It is therefore not safe to reject conjunto solely because the intended meaning is team.

groups.title: país · nacional · gobierno · social · estado · público · político

sections.title: Country, state and government
sections.text: País commonly names a country or territory. Estado can name a political organization or a constituent state of a federation. Gobierno can name the governing body or the action of governing.

sections.title: Related adjectives and people
sections.text: Nacional relates to a nation; social to society or association; político to politics. Público can mean public, state-run, open to all or known openly, depending on context. As a noun, político/política can refer to a politician.

sections.title: Sequence and unfolding
sections.text: Proceso describes successive phases or steps. Desarrollo describes development, growth or the unfolding of something. Development does not always mean improvement.

sections.title: Change and a planned undertaking
sections.text: Cambio means a change; proyecto is a plan or project. A project can contain a process and undergo changes; the terms describe different aspects rather than mutually exclusive objects.
examples: There is a change of plans.

groups.title: historia · cuenta · palabra · información · relación · tema

sections.title: Story, account and relationship
sections.text: Historia can mean history or a story. Relación can mean a connection, relationship or an account/list. Cuenta can mean an account, bill or calculation.

sections.title: Topic, information and word
sections.text: Tema identifies what something is about. Información is communicated or acquired knowledge. Palabra is a word and can also refer to someone’s promise or turn to speak.

sections.title: Noun and verb
sections.text: Vida is the noun life. Vivir means live and can describe being alive or residing somewhere. Existir means exist and can apply to people, things or possibilities.

sections.title: Experiences and livelihood
sections.text: Vivir can also mean experience something. Vivir de names what provides a livelihood or sustenance. These uses are not conveyed simply by existir.

sections.title: Always, never and every
sections.text: Siempre expresses always; nunca never. Cada distributes over members or intervals. Cada día and todos los días can both mean every day.

sections.title: Position of nunca
sections.text: Nunca before a verb can provide the negation itself. After a verb it commonly appears with no. Both patterns express a single negative meaning.

sections.title: Combining positives and negatives
sections.text: Y joins elements; o offers alternatives and can also introduce an alternative name. Ni coordinates negatives. Spanish can combine no and ni without canceling the negative meaning.
examples: I don’t want tea or coffee.
Neither Ana nor Luis is coming.

sections.title: Without and not even
sections.text: Sin introduces what is absent and can take a noun or infinitive. Ni can also intensify a negative as not even.
examples: She didn’t even look at me.

sections.title: Start, endpoint and interval
sections.text: Desde marks a starting point; hasta an endpoint; durante a period; entre can mark the bounds of an interval. These relationships can all involve time but are different.
examples: Desde las dos hasta las cuatro.
Entre las dos y las cuatro.

sections.title: Other uses of hasta
sections.text: Hasta can mean even. In some American varieties, affirmative time expressions with hasta can mean not until rather than continuation until. Interpret these with local usage and context; a bare translation until is not sufficient for every case.

groups.title: como · así · forma · manera · sistema · medio

sections.title: How and in this way
sections.text: Como can introduce a manner comparison or the way something happens; cómo asks how. Así means in this/that way. Forma and manera can name a way of doing something.
examples: Do it as I explained to you.

sections.title: Means and an organized system
sections.text: Medio can name a means used to reach an end. Sistema can name an organized set or method. Both can relate to how something is done, but medio need not be an organized procedure.

sections.title: Position in a sequence
sections.text: Primero, segundo and último identify sequence positions. Before a masculine singular noun, primero becomes primer. Adjectival forms agree with their nouns.

sections.title: Relative order and first of all
sections.text: Antes and después locate something relative to something else. Primero can stand as an adverb for the first step, without a noun.
examples: First I read; afterward I write.

sections.title: Instrument and channel
sections.text: Con can name a companion or instrument. Por can name a channel or means of communication. The object and construction matter when English uses with or by.

sections.title: Other uses are broader
sections.text: Con also introduces circumstances or contents; por has uses including cause, route and exchange. Avoid assigning either word a single English equivalent.
examples: She did it out of fear.

sections.title: Today and now
sections.text: Hoy points to the current day. Ahora points to the current moment or period. Both can extend to a broader present, so the day/moment contrast is useful but not absolute.

sections.title: A broader present
sections.text: Hoy en día means nowadays. Ahora can contrast the current situation with an earlier one, even when the change spans years.
examples: Hoy en día mucha gente trabaja desde casa.
Nowadays many people work from home.
Antes vivía en Lima; ahora vivo en Madrid.
I used to live in Lima; now I live in Madrid.

sections.title: Remembering and knowing
sections.text: Saber says knowledge is possessed; recordar presents keeping or bringing something to mind. These can overlap when asking about information retained in memory.

sections.title: Remember and remind
sections.text: Standard recordar takes a direct object; acordarse takes de. Recordar can also mean remind someone. Regional recordarse de is documented, particularly in parts of Central America; it is not the general pattern taught here.

sections.title: A year and an age
sections.text: Año is masculine, with plural años. Spanish expresses age with tener + a number of years.

sections.title: Counting
sections.text: Dos means two and has the same form with masculine and feminine nouns. Segundo means second: it gives a position rather than a count.

sections.title: New in different senses
sections.text: Nuevo can mean newly made, not previously used, or different from what there was before. Something nuevo for a person need not be newly manufactured. De nuevo means again.

sections.title: World and a sphere of experience
sections.text: Mundo can mean the world or human society, and also a particular sphere of life. Todo el mundo means everyone in ordinary use.
examples: She traveled all over the world.

sections.title: House and home
sections.text: Casa can mean a house or the home someone lives in, including an apartment. Hogar also means home and can refer to the household or family. Avoid a strict building-versus-feelings rule.
examples: They want to establish a home together.

sections.title: Counting and time
sections.text: Tres means three; tercero means third. In a clock expression, las tres means three o’clock.

sections.title: A broad word for a thing
sections.text: Cosa can refer to a physical object, a matter or an abstract idea. It is feminine regardless of what the thing itself is.
examples: I have something to tell you.

sections.title: Feminine despite the ending
sections.text: Mano meaning hand is feminine: la mano, las manos. A mano means by hand; echar una mano means lend a hand or help.
examples: I wrote the letter by hand.
Can you give me a hand?

sections.title: According to and depending on
sections.text: Según can introduce a source or a rule. With a clause it can also express dependence on how things turn out. After según, Spanish uses subject pronouns such as yo and tú, rather than mí and ti.
examples: According to Ana, it is true.
In your view, it is enough.

sections.title: One singular form for both genders
sections.text: Importante stays the same with a masculine or feminine singular noun; the plural is importantes. It describes importance, which need not mean size or urgency.

sections.title: A number that is a noun
sections.text: Millón is a masculine noun, plural millones. When it directly precedes what is counted, use de: un millón de personas. It can also exaggerate a very large number.

sections.title: Father, dad and parents
sections.text: Padre can name a father or a man acting as a father. Papá is the familiar dad form. Padres can mean fathers or parents, depending on context. Padre also has a religious title use.

sections.title: Problem and difficulty
sections.text: Problema is masculine despite its ending: el problema. It can be an obstacle or a question to solve. Dificultad overlaps for an obstacle, but also describes the degree of difficulty or trouble in doing something.

sections.title: A person who presides
sections.text: Presidente can refer to the head of a country, organization, meeting or other body. For a woman, presidenta and la presidente are both valid.

sections.title: Opposition
sections.text: Contra can mean against in opposition or confrontation. En contra de is another construction for opposition. Con, meaning with, describes a different relationship.
examples: Está en contra de la propuesta.

sections.title: A city
sections.text: Ciudad is feminine, plural ciudades. It names a city; it can also refer to urban life in contrast to the countryside.
examples: I live in a small city.

sections.title: A month
sections.text: Mes is masculine, plural meses. Cada mes means every month; al mes can express a monthly rate or frequency.
examples: We see each other every month.

sections.title: Politics and sport
sections.text: Partido can name a political party or a sporting match. Encuentro overlaps in the match sense. Juego names a game or play more broadly and, in tennis, a game within a set; these sports terms do not always name the same unit.

sections.title: Night and this evening
sections.text: Noche is feminine. Esta noche can mean tonight or this evening; an exact English evening/night boundary is not built into the phrase. Buenas noches is used both in greeting and in parting.

sections.title: Feminine with el
sections.text: Agua is feminine. Immediately before the singular noun, use el because its first a is stressed. The adjective is still feminine: el agua fría. Use feminine esta and mucha: esta agua, mucha agua. Un, algún and ningún also occur directly before agua. The plural takes las: las aguas.
examples: I need a lot of water.

sections.title: Here and the nearby area
sections.text: Aquí and acá can both mean here, including movement toward here. Acá also refers to the nearby area and combines with degree words, as in más acá. Do not impose a universal stationary-aquí versus movement-acá rule.

sections.title: Company and undertaking
sections.text: Empresa can mean a business or an undertaking requiring effort. Compañía overlaps for a business, but also means companionship or a group such as a theater company.

sections.title: Losing and missing
sections.text: Perder can mean lose a possession or contest, and miss transport or an opportunity. Perderse can mean get lost. It changes e to ie in forms such as pierdo.

sections.title: Opening
sections.text: Abrir can take the thing being opened as its object. A place can abrir when it opens for business; abrirse can describe something opening. Its participle is abierto.
examples: La tienda abre a las nueve.

sections.title: Service and other contexts
sections.text: Servicio can name an action that serves or assists, an organized service, or facilities for a purpose. It has specialized senses; for example, servicio can also mean a toilet or bathroom.

sections.title: General and overall
sections.text: General describes what is common or applies broadly. Global can describe something taken as a whole, and also something worldwide. En general means generally; global is not an automatic replacement in that expression.
examples: An overall view of the problem.

sections.title: An instance or a model
sections.text: Ejemplo can be an instance illustrating something or a model to follow. Por ejemplo means for example; dar ejemplo can mean set an example.
examples: For example, we can go tomorrow.

sections.title: Mother and mom
sections.text: Madre can name a mother or a woman acting as a mother. Mamá is the familiar mom form. Madre also has extended uses for an origin or source; mamá does not automatically replace those.

sections.title: A book
sections.text: Libro is masculine, plural libros. It can be a physical or electronic book, and also a division of a longer work. The word does not require paper.
examples: I am reading an electronic book.

sections.title: Family as a collective noun
sections.text: Familia is feminine singular even when it refers to several relatives. It can also name a group of related things. Plural familias names multiple families.

sections.title: Health and a wish
sections.text: Salud is feminine. Tener buena salud means be in good health. ¡Salud! can be a toast or a wish for someone’s health, including after a sneeze.

sections.title: A week
sections.text: Semana is feminine, plural semanas. It can mean a calendar week or a period of seven days. El fin de semana means the weekend.
examples: I am coming back next week.

sections.title: A right and the law
sections.text: As a masculine noun, derecho can mean an entitlement or law as a field. Tener derecho a + noun or infinitive means have the right to something or to do something. Adjectival derecho and directional derecha have other meanings.
examples: I have the right to enter.

sections.title: Writing to someone
sections.text: Escribir can take the text written as a direct object and a + person for its recipient. Its irregular participle is escrito.
examples: I write a letter to Ana.

sections.title: Body and an organized body
sections.text: Cuerpo can name a person’s or animal’s body. It also has extended senses for the main body of a work or an organized group.

sections.title: Economic and inexpensive
sections.text: Económico can relate to the economy or describe something inexpensive. Its meaning depends on the noun and context; it does not always translate as economic.

sections.title: An eye and a warning
sections.text: Ojo is masculine, plural ojos. ¡Ojo! is also a warning to be careful or pay attention.

sections.title: Counting
sections.text: Cuatro means four, with the same form for masculine and feminine nouns. Cuarto means fourth, identifying a position rather than a count.

sections.title: Later and next
sections.text: Both words can place something later in time or next in a sequence. The surrounding sentence establishes the sequence and timing.
examples: First we eat, then we talk.
First we eat, then we talk.

sections.title: After a named event
sections.text: Después de takes a noun or an infinitive. Luego de also means after, with regional variation. The DLE specifically records luego de in Argentina, Mexico and the Dominican Republic.

sections.title: After something happens
sections.text: Después que and después de que both introduce a clause meaning after. Luego que and luego de que are also valid. The DPD describes these luego constructions as just after, and the DLE glosses luego que as as soon as.
examples: Después de que terminó la reunión, salimos.
After the meeting ended, we left.
Luego que terminó la reunión, salimos.
As soon as the meeting ended, we left.

sections.title: How much later
sections.text: Después combines with mucho, bastante and un poco to express the size of a time gap.

sections.title: Order and ranking
sections.text: Después also describes position in an order, hierarchy or preference. This can be a ranking rather than a later event.
examples: Después de Ana, Luis es el mejor jugador.
After Ana, Luis is the best player.

sections.title: Luego can mean therefore
sections.text: As a conjunction, luego introduces a conclusion. Replacing it with después changes the relationship to time or order.
examples: Todos votaron a favor, luego hay acuerdo.
Everyone voted in favor, therefore there is agreement.

sections.title: Regional meanings
sections.text: Luego can also mean promptly or right away in regions including Mexico, Chile and the Canary Islands. In El Salvador, the DLE also records quickly and early. Interpret it with the local usage and context.

sections.title: Expressions to learn together
sections.text: These expressions have meanings of their own.
examples: Después de todo lo que hice, se queja.
After everything I did, she complains.
sections.note: The final example adds a sense of despite that effort.
